newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU needs effective foreign policy, Bildt says.
newsitem.headline: EU needs effective foreign policy, Bildt says.

text.p: The European Union must set up effective foreign policy structures to deal with Southeast Europe, which will remain its biggest foreign policy challenge, the international envoy for Bosnia, Carl Bildt, said on Tuesday

"We now have a belt of poverty and despair across the Balkan peninsula, stretching from Bosnia, Montenegro and Albania through Serbia and Macedonia into Bulgaria and Romania. And this could breed and fuel further social and political instability," Bildt said in a speech marking the end of his term of office.

The major powers involved in Bosnia peace efforts -- the United States, France, Germany, Russia and Britain -- are expected to appoint a successor to the former Swedish prime minister on Friday. Diplomats have named Spain's ambassador to the United Nations, Carlos Westendorp, as a leading candidate.

Bildt urged European Union leaders who will hold a summit meeting in Amsterdam next month to put machinery in place which would allow the bloc to play a full diplomatic role in Southeast Europe alongside the United States and Russia.

The bloc's Council of Ministers should remain the focal point of the EU's efforts to develop a common foreign and security policy, he said in a speech to the Netherlands Association for International Affairs.
Bildt said it was important to involve the Western European Union (WEU) military grouping in EU foreign and security policy.

"There should be integration with the Western European Union when it comes to setting up structures to prepare and implement policy and to ensure that there is the ability to talk to and within NATO with competence and clarity on these issues."
Many European Union members, led by France and Germany, favour the full incorporation of the WEU into the EU, but neutral EU members such as Ireland and Sweden oppose this.
Bildt said a coherent security structure for the Balkan region would require the stationing of external forces in key areas to deter any attempt to resort to aggression.
